newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Peseta shrugs off Spain's surprise rate cut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Peseta shrugs off Spain's surprise rate cut.

text.p: The Bank of Spain's surprise cut in its official rate did little to take the steam out of the peseta on Thursday and economists said it would take a lot more to tame the buoyant currency.
The central bank caught markets unawares by shaving 25 basis points off its key money market rate to 6.00 percent at its regular repurchase auction.

"A 25 basis point cut in this kind of environment doesn't do anything to the currency, it may even have been seen as a sign of confidence that inflation is under control which will help boost the peseta," said Luca Jellinek, analyst at Banque Paribas in London.
By 1515 GMT, the peseta was trading at 83.52 per mark, slightly firmer than levels seen just prior to the cut at around 83.61 and compared to late Wednesday levels of 83.67.

Economists said since expectations for further rate cuts would attract overseas funds into domestic bond and equity assets because of higher returns currently available, the peseta would continue to remain firm.

"Expectations for further aggressive cuts means it makes sense to invest in peseta (assets) and there's no real reason to reverse positions at the moment," said Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Societe Generale in Madrid

Considerable inflows into Spain's bond and equity markets, sparked partly by the belief that Spain will be in the first wave to join Europe's monetary union (EMU), have already exerted significant pressure on the peseta to appreciate.

But in recent months, the peseta has remained at the mercy of the central bank which was thought to be keen to hold the currency in the 84.00 to 85.00 per mark band in the run-up to a single European currency.
Last Friday, however, the Spanish currency slammed through the 84.00 per mark barrier to levels not seen since May, after the central bank relaxed its stance and refrained from intervening.
Some traders had interpreted the central bank's absence from the currency market as a sign that it intended to turn to other means to control the currency, namely interest rates.
However economists said such a policy would not be effective in the short-term and it would take a number of hefty cuts before the central bank achieved the desired effect.

"Rate cuts will not initially effect the currency because it's moving of its own accord, for other reasons, but obviously if you start slashing rates then eventually you will stop the peseta from appreciating," said Jellinek.
Economists said the market was discounting a series of aggressive interest rate cuts for 1997, which by the end of the year may succeed in bringing the currency back toward the 84.00 per mark level.
"Spanish rates have quite a bit to go yet and according to interest rate futures, the market is pricing in a Bank of Spain repo rate of around five percent in June," said Urrutia.
Some economists pointed out, however, that Thursday's cut had in the meantime succeeded in easing some of the pressure on forward exchange rates.
"There are some signs of easing in the forward market, and people are not pressing as hard as they were a couple of days ago," said one trader.
Until the next rate cut, traders said they expected the peseta to remain largely rangebound and did not expect to see further intervention from the central bank.
